also: I say yes, you say no

terms.comment: The plainest yes; stronger, ita vērō, ita prōrsus (Lewis & Short). Most often, though, Latin answers with no particle at all: it repeats the word the question turns on (Traupman 250), Vēnitne? — Vēnit. (Plaut. Bacch. 247).

evidence: Plaut. Amph. 544–544b: numquid vīs? — Etiam: ut āctūtum adveniās.
Cic. Ac. 2.104: aut etiam aut nōn respondēre possit
terms.comment: Cicero’s word for the bare yes of a yes-or-no answer.

evidence: Plaut. Ps. 664–664b: Quīn ubi pranderō, dabō operam somnō. — Sānē cēnseō.
Plaut. Poen. 1079–1079b: sed tē monērī num nevīs? — Sānē volō.
terms.comment: The yes that grants or approves: “yes, do”, “yes, I’d like that”.

terms.register: in this sense, vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.
evidence: Ter. Ad. 609b–609c: Sequere mē ergō hāc intrō. — Maximē.
Plaut. Most. 1009–1009b: operam mihi dā. — Maximē.
terms.comment: The willing yes to a request or an order; its pair is Minimē!, not at all (see no way!).

terms.register: in this sense, vōx cōmica: often in Plautus, twice in Terence
terms.comment: Cicero names Admodum and Prōrsus ita est as the yeses said in conversation to let it move on (Leg. 3.26, quoted by Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Quid ais? an vēnit Pamphilus? — Vēnit. — Dīs grātiam habeō.
phrases.english: What did you say? Has Pamphilus come? — He has. — Thank the gods.

phrases.latin: quid istīc tibi negōtī est? — Mihine? — Ita.
phrases.english: What business have you in there? — Me? — Yes, you.

phrases.latin: Quīn ubi pranderō, dabō operam somnō. — Sānē cēnseō.
phrases.english: After lunch I’ll have a nap. — Yes, do.

phrases.latin: Tū, Parmenō, hūc fac illī addūcantur. — Maximē.
phrases.english: “Parmeno, see that they are brought here.” “Certainly.”
Someone says no? I say no. Says yes? I say yes.
I say yes, you say no.
